chunks.text: The Indian Ocean trade was the largest and richest maritime trading network of the period c. 1200–1450. It connected East Africa, Arabia, Persia, India, Southeast Asia, and China, moving more goods than the overland Silk Roads.

The monsoon winds reverse direction with the seasons, broadly blowing from the northeast in winter and the southwest in summer. Because this pattern was reliable and well understood, sailors could plan round-trip voyages, riding the wind out in one season and home in the next.

Mastery of monsoon knowledge was the foundational technology of Indian Ocean trade. It shows that environmental understanding, not just machinery, could power long-distance commerce, since sailors timed entire voyages to the seasonal wind reversal.

A ship can carry many tons of cargo at a fraction of the cost per pound of a camel's few hundred pounds. This meant the Indian Ocean network could profitably carry bulkier, heavier, cheaper goods that the overland Silk Roads could not, such as large quantities of textiles, timber, and foodstuffs.

The lateen sail was a triangular sail that allowed ships to sail at an angle to the wind rather than only straight downwind. It gave captains far more control and was a key maritime technology of Indian Ocean trade.

The Arab dhow used lateen sails, while the massive Chinese junk had multiple masts and watertight compartments that kept it afloat even if part of the hull was breached. Both could carry large cargoes across open water.

Indian Ocean navigation improved with the magnetic compass, a Chinese invention that diffused westward, and the astrolabe, which let sailors estimate their latitude from the stars. Better maps and knowledge of currents and coasts also aided voyages.

Goods traded across the Indian Ocean included Indian cotton textiles (especially from Gujarat) and pepper, Southeast Asian spices like cloves and nutmeg, Chinese silk and porcelain, East African gold, ivory, and enslaved people, and Arabian incense and horses. Bulk transport let even ordinary goods enter long-distance trade.
India produced cotton textiles in enormous quantities, especially in Gujarat, and these cloths were prized throughout the Indian Ocean world. Indian textiles were a major bulk export of the network.

On the East African coast, the Swahili city-states of Kilwa, Mombasa, and Mogadishu flourished as gateways connecting the African interior to the Indian Ocean. They exported gold, ivory, and enslaved people and grew wealthy from trade.

Major Indian Ocean trading hubs included Gujarat and Calicut on India's coasts, Malacca commanding the strait between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, and Hormuz and Aden controlling the entrances to the Persian Gulf and Red Sea. These ports grew rich from their positions on the network.

The port of Malacca commanded the strategic strait between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, growing rich by taxing the trade that had to pass through it. It was a key chokepoint of the Indian Ocean network.

Indian Ocean port cities were cosmopolitan places where merchants from across the ocean met and mingled, including African, Arab, Persian, Indian, Chinese, and Southeast Asian traders. Their prosperity flowed directly from their position on the trade network.

Diasporic communities were colonies of merchants living far from their homelands, scattered along the trade routes. Because round-trip voyages depended on the monsoon, merchants often waited months in foreign ports and many settled permanently, founding such communities.

Arab and Persian merchants settled in the Swahili city-states of East Africa, Gujarati Indian merchants established communities in Southeast Asia and on the African coast, and Chinese merchants settled in Southeast Asian ports. These diaspora communities were the human infrastructure of Indian Ocean trade.

Diasporic merchants intermarried with local people, introduced their languages and technologies, and spread their religion. They turned trade routes into channels of cultural and religious diffusion around the Indian Ocean rim.

The greatest cultural consequence of Indian Ocean trade was the spread of Islam around the entire ocean rim. Muslim merchants carried their faith to the Swahili coast, the trading cities of India, and Southeast Asia, where Malacca embraced Islam around 1400 and helped seed the Muslim societies of Indonesia.

The Swahili civilization of the East African coast was a direct product of Indian Ocean diaspora contacts. Its language blended Bantu African roots with Arabic loanwords, and its elite was Muslim, reflecting centuries of trade-driven cultural blending.

Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming Dynasty sent the admiral Zheng He on seven grand expeditions across the Indian Ocean, reaching Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and the East African coast. The fleets had hundreds of ships, tens of thousands of men, and 'treasure ships' far larger than European vessels of the time.

The Ming treasure voyages of Zheng He were not expeditions of conquest or colonization. Their main aim was to display the power and glory of Ming China, overawe foreign rulers, and draw them into the Chinese tributary system, collecting tribute and exotic gifts such as a giraffe for the emperor.

After 1433 China abruptly ended the treasure voyages and dismantled the fleet, because the expeditions were enormously expensive, Confucian officials disapproved of them, and China faced renewed threats on its northern land frontier. China chose to turn inward.

China's withdrawal from the Indian Ocean after 1433 left the network without a single dominant power, creating a vacuum that European powers, beginning with the Portuguese around 1500, would later fill. China had the capability to dominate the ocean and chose not to.

During the period c. 1200–1450, Europeans did not dominate the Indian Ocean; they had not yet arrived. The network was run by African, Arab, Persian, Indian, Chinese, and Southeast Asian merchants long before Portuguese ships entered it around 1500.

The Silk Roads carried high-value luxuries by camel because overland transport was expensive, while the Indian Ocean's cheaper ship transport carried both luxuries and bulkier goods like textiles, timber, and foodstuffs. Both networks spread Islam, but the Indian Ocean spread it especially through diasporic merchant communities.
